title: Lower cardinality estimate for substring-match table filters
reasons: abandoned by the implementer after investigation
summary:
I was stopped before I could check this change, so it is not ready to judge. There are no before/after numbers: `bench` and EXPLAIN were never run on the new build. The final working tree's build was still running when I had to stop, so I don't know if it compiles. An earlier build with most of the change (before I removed an unused helper and wired up relation_manager.cpp) printed BUILD OK.

What the code does:
- **Header** (`relation_statistics_helper.hpp`): adds `SUBSTRING_MATCH_SELECTIVITY = DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY * DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY` (0.04). Also adds two static helpers: `IsSubstringMatchPredicate(const Expression&)` and `IsSubstringMatchFilter(const TableFilter&)`.
- **Predicate test** (`relation_statistics_helper.cpp`): `IsSubstringMatchPredicate` is true for `contains(x, <non-empty VARCHAR constant>)`, and for `~~` / `like_escape` whose constant pattern starts with '%' and has at least one character other than '%' or '_'. It also looks inside CONJUNCTION_AND. It never matches OR, NOT or `!~~`. `IsSubstringMatchFilter` checks ExpressionFilter and ConjunctionAndFilter table filters the same way.
- **Scan estimate** (`ExtractGetStats`): when no equality filter fired and some non-optional table filter is a substring match, the estimate is base_cardinality * 0.04 instead of * 0.2.
- **Unpushed filters** (`relation_manager.cpp`): a static `GetDatasourceFilterSelectivity` replaces the five DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY uses for LogicalFilters left above a scan. It returns 0.04 if any of their expressions is a substring match, otherwise 0.2.

Baseline I did check: EXPLAIN of q09 estimates ~1,256,266 rows for lineitem⋈part⋈orders and ~5,057,324 for the top join. The part filter is pushed into the scan as `contains(p_name, 'ghost')`, so the table-filter path is the one that matters.
notes: To finish: 1) run `dbe-tool build` and confirm the current tree compiles; 2) EXPLAIN q09.m0 and check that the scan estimate on part falls from ~40,000 to ~8,000 and whether the join order changes; 3) run the full `dbe-tool bench`. If results are mixed, try the issue's fallback of applying the lower selectivity only when the literal is at least 3 characters. Shell notes: python3, compound commands that `cd` first, and piping into grep all needed permission approval here, so make edits with the Edit tool and use absolute paths. Changing the header triggers a long rebuild (over 10 minutes), so run builds in the background.

title: Substring-match scan selectivity (minimal, finish E0001)
reasons: abandoned by the implementer after investigation
summary:
I built the change but it did not alter q09's plan, so I'm abandoning it. In relation_statistics_helper.cpp I added a file-local IsSubstringMatchFilter. It matches contains(col, non-empty VARCHAR constant), and ~~/like_escape with a constant pattern that starts with '%' and has a literal character; it recurses into AND conjunctions. When no equality filter applied and a non-optional filter matches, the scan estimate uses selectivity 0.04 instead of DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY (0.2). The build passed.

The estimates moved as intended: in EXPLAIN, the lineitem⋈part⋈orders estimate fell from about 1.26M to about 241k, and the top join from about 5.06M to about 1.01M. The physical plan stayed the same. The hypothesis misread the plan: in DuckDB's hash join the left child is the probe side and the right child is the build side. orders (1.5M, cut to about 300k rows by its bloom filter) and partsupp (800k) are already the probe sides, and the filtered part/lineitem side (about 324k) is already the build side, so there was nothing to flip.

Quick bench, 4 hot runs per query (best → yours): q09 121.2 → 114.4 ms (−5.6%), q13 +0.5%, q14 −1.1%, q16 +0.2%. Since the plan did not change, the q09 difference is noise (the tool says differences under about 5% are noise). The edit is still in the working tree because my attempt to revert it with git checkout was blocked. Please discard it.
notes:
E0001/this experiment's premise is false: q09 already builds on the 324k filtered side and probes orders and partsupp, since in DuckDB's HASH_JOIN the left child is the probe and the right child is the build. Most of q09's time is in the hash join probes: about 0.18–0.20s for the probe of orders (300k rows after the bloom filter) and about 0.14–0.16s for the two-key probe of partsupp (800k rows), plus 0.43s on the lineitem scan. Ideas worth trying instead:
(a) Push a bloom filter (BF) built from the 324k build side down into the partsupp scan. Its Dynamic Filters currently show only min/max ranges, while orders gets an "IN BF" filter. Multi-key joins may not get a BF pushdown.
(b) Lower the per-row cost of the hash join probe or of materializing its payload.
The selectivity change itself is harmless and only touches estimates, but it has no measured gain here, so it should not be resubmitted without a query that actually changes plan.

title: Cardinality-aware perfect hash aggregation above the bit threshold
reasons: abandoned by the implementer after investigation
summary:
I tried a cost-based acceptance rule in CanUsePerfectHashAggregate (plan_aggregate.cpp only). When perfect_hash_bits is above perfect_ht_threshold, it still accepts perfect hashing up to a 20-bit cap if total thread-local slots (2^bits * threads) <= k * child.estimated_cardinality. The tree builds, but I'm abandoning: the planner's estimates can't tell the case that wins from the case that loses.

1) The issue's rule (k=2) never fires on q13. The aggregate's child estimate is ~300k rows (default LIKE selectivity on a filtered side of a RIGHT join), while the actual input is 1.53M. On 8 threads, 2^18*8 = 2.1M > 600k.

2) I loosened k to 8 so q13 qualifies. Full bench against best:
- Faster: q13 -24.1% (97.4 -> 73.9 ms), q02 -17%, q03 -10%, q07 -11%. Many of these are probably noise; it was a quick 4-run check.
- Slower: q17 +63.8% (20.5 -> 33.6 ms) and q14 +13.5%.
- Geomean: -2.1%, below the 2.7% bar, and q17 breaks the 10% per-template limit.

In q17 the aggregate in the decorrelated subquery sits on a join estimated at ~6M rows that actually yields 5,850 rows. It gets an 18-bit PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY, and every thread allocates, initialises and combines 262k slots for almost no rows. So q13 needs a rule loose enough to forgive a 5x underestimate, and q17 shows a 1000x overestimate that the same rule lets through.

Other measurements:
- Forced perfect hashing (SET perfect_ht_threshold=18) on q13's inner aggregate: ~115 -> ~90 ms wall. The hypothesis itself is right.
- 20-bit perfect hashing on an empty input (6M-row estimate): ~10 ms extra over the hash path on 8 threads.
notes:
- Do not retry a planner-only, estimate-based threshold for perfect hash aggregation. q13 is underestimated about 5x and q17 is overestimated about 1000x, so no factor separates them.
- A workable version needs runtime adaptivity in the operator. In PhysicalPerfectHashAggregate / PerfectAggregateHashTable, every local state eagerly allocates and InitializeStates all 2^bits slots in its constructor, and Combine and Destroy loop over all slots serially. Options:
  (a) Initialise states lazily: only zero group_is_set, and initialise a slot's state on first touch in AddChunk.
  (b) Have Combine iterate only over touched slots (track a touched list, or fall back once it gets dense).
  (c) Start with the radix hash table and switch to the perfect table once the observed input/groups ratio justifies it.
  With (a) and (b), the cost for small inputs becomes O(touched groups) plus one memset of 2^bits bytes, and a bit-threshold rule ignoring cardinality (bits <= 18-20) could then be safe. That touches the operator .cpp and probably a header.
- Check q17 in particular for any change in this area, since it is the template that regresses.
- Measured on 8 threads: forced 18-bit perfect hashing on q13's inner aggregate ~115 -> ~90 ms; 20-bit perfect table on an empty input ~10 ms over the hash path.

title: Lazy-initialised perfect hash aggregate table with a bounded bit extension
reasons: train geomean changed by -0.3%; the bar requires at least -2.7%
summary:
Fixed the review finding: `perfect_ht_threshold` now limits perfect hashing again. In CanUsePerfectHashAggregate (plan_aggregate.cpp), the 18-bit/4MB-per-thread extension only applies while the setting is at its default (compared with StringUtil::ToUnsigned(PerfectHtThresholdSetting::DefaultValue)). When the user changes the value, it is a hard upper bound on bits, so 0 or 1 turns perfect hashing off. The lazy-initialisation changes in perfect_aggregate_hashtable.cpp/.hpp from the earlier attempt are unchanged; the reviewer found no problem with them. States are initialised on first touch in AddChunk and Combine, there is a touched counter with an early return in Combine, Scan and Combine skip unset flags 8 bytes at a time, and Destroy only visits set slots.

The build passes. There is no unittest runner here, so I could not run the three requested test files directly. Instead I reproduced their plan checks with `dbe-tool sql` on a 16-bit no-stats key: at the default it plans PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY, with threshold 0 or 1 it plans HASH_GROUP_BY (what perfect_ht.test lines 17-33 and test_filter_clause:428 rely on), and with threshold 20 it plans perfect (what test_perfect_ht.test sets). I also read the other plan-regex tests (union_single_dedup, issue8505); they still match because `HASH_GROUP_BY` is a substring of `PERFECT_HASH_GROUP_BY`.

Full bench against the current best: geomean -3.0% (an earlier quick run gave +0.6%, with q03 and q14 noisy). q13 is about -19% on both full runs (95->77ms), q09 -8%, q17 -6.8%, q18 -3.6%. q14 showed +12% and +24% in two runs, but its plan has no grouped aggregate, and a third run gave -1.8%, so that was noise.
notes: The extension now applies only while the setting is at its default value. If a user explicitly sets 12 (the default), it is treated as default and the extension applies; I accepted that because the engine does not expose whether a setting was explicitly set. The harness gives no way to run sqllogictests, so those checks were reproduced with dbe-tool sql. Bench noise is about ±10% per query on quick runs, and the geomean landed at -3.0%, close to the 2.7% bar. The real gain is concentrated in q13. Possible follow-up: tune the 4MB cap, or base acceptance on observed cardinality at runtime.

title: Per-key bloom filter pushdown for multi-key hash joins
reasons: abandoned by the implementer after investigation
summary: Implemented per-key bloom filters for multi-key equality hash joins. JoinHashTable::key_bloom_filters (indexed by condition index) is initialised in AllocatePointerTable and filled in Finalize by gathering layout column cond_idx, running VectorOperations::Hash on it and inserting the hashes. CanUseBloomFilter now allows conditions.size()>1. The deferred entries carry cond_idx through a new JoinFilterDeferredBloomFilter struct, and PushBloomFilter uses that condition's BF, null semantics, name and type. It builds (BUILD OK). The profile of q09.m0 shows the premise is wrong. In the 2-key join (p_partkey=ps_partkey AND l_suppkey=ps_suppkey), partsupp (800k rows) is the BUILD side and the lineitem/part pipeline (324,507 rows) is the PROBE side. A key BF would go into the lineitem scan, which the part join has already filtered, and the probe-larger-than-build check rejects it anyway. The partsupp scan still shows only the ps_suppkey min/max filter from the supplier join. Bench vs best, full run: geomean +6.7% slower (q19 +48%, q22 +21%, q18 +20%, q09 +4.8%). Re-run of q09/q18/q19/q22: +5.9%/+2.5%/+9.9%/+4.0%, geomean +5.5%. No template got faster.
notes: The issue's hypothesis is wrong: in q09 partsupp is the build side of the 2-key join, not the probe. A real win for q09's partsupp cost would need the planner to flip the join sides, or a semi-join filter from the lineitem/part side pushed into the partsupp scan (sideways information passing up the build side). The bloom-filter pushdown in this engine only reaches probe-side scans. The per-key BF code is correct as far as I can tell (condition i equals layout column i; reordering of equality conditions already happens in PhysicalComparisonJoin, and join_condition indices refer to op.conditions == ht->conditions). It could be revived if a workload with a filtered, smaller build side on a composite key appears. Also note the probe 324k vs build 800k ratio: the join operator (0.26s CPU) is dominated by building an 800k-row HT from the partsupp side.

title: Collapse adjacent duplicate group keys before hash-table probe in aggregation
reasons: abandoned by the implementer after investigation
summary:
I built the run-head collapse in GroupedAggregateHashTable::FindOrCreateGroupsInternal and it works, but q18 does not get measurably faster, so I'm abandoning it.

What it does: a file-local helper finds rows whose group is identical to the row before. It checks the hash first, then each group column through the existing UnifiedVectorFormat. NULLs must match, values are compared bit for bit, and strings use string_t ==. Supported types are numerics, hugeint/uhugeint, float/double, interval and varchar; any other group type turns the check off. If at least 1/8 of the chunk are duplicates, only the run heads are probed (through the existing HAS_SEL inner loop), and afterwards each duplicate copies its head's address. Over a 16-chunk trial, if fewer than half the chunks benefit, the check is turned off for that table. The bookkeeping (a heads SelectionVector and counters) lives in AggregateHTAppendState in the header.

It builds (BUILD OK). Spot checks gave the expected results: the q18 subquery returns 10 rows; GROUP BY on (orderkey, linenumber) gives 6,001,215 groups whose counts sum to the input; a GROUP BY with NULL keys returns a correct NULL group; a varchar plus boolean key works.

Measurements:
- **Aggregate CPU:** EXPLAIN ANALYZE puts HASH_GROUP_BY at 0.83s before and 0.75s after, summed over threads, about 10% less.
- **q18 wall time:** across four bench runs the change was -2.1%, -5.4%, -0.9% and +1.5%, about -1.7% on average. That is inside the stated noise of about 5% and far from the predicted -15 to -25%.
- **Geomean:** the full-suite numbers (-2.6% and -5.0%) were also noise. Queries that barely aggregate moved the same amount, and a rerun of q03, q14, q18 and q19 came out at +0.6%.
notes:
The premise was wrong. A duplicate row next to its run head was already cheap: its probe hits the same table slot and group row the head had just touched, so both are in cache, and the salt and RowMatcher compare cost little. Most of the aggregate's time is not in probing repeat rows. It goes to creating 1.5M new groups (append, partitioning, InitializeStates), UpdateAggregates, and the combine/finalize phase for 1.5M groups. Removing the probes for about 75% of rows saved roughly 10% of the aggregate's CPU and almost no wall time.

If someone picks this up again:
1. Profile how sink time splits against combine/finalize for high-cardinality aggregates before attacking the probe.
2. For clustered input, a bigger saving might come from pre-aggregating each run (summing payloads inside a run before updating state, so the state is touched once per run), but UpdateAggregates is generic across aggregate functions, which makes that harder.
3. Look at the cost of the partitioned append and of the finalize phase for 1.5M groups.

The diff is saved for the record. It is correct and low risk if a later change makes the probe the bottleneck.

title: Contains-filter scan selectivity to flip q09 build sides at SF10
summary:
In src/optimizer/join_order/relation_statistics_helper.cpp, I added a file-local `IsContainsFilter(const TableFilter&)`. It matches an ExpressionFilter whose expression is a BoundFunctionExpression named "contains" with 2 children, where the second child is a non-NULL VARCHAR constant of at least 3 bytes. It also recurses into ConjunctionAndFilter children. When a scan has no equality filter and a non-optional filter is a contains filter, ExtractGetStats now uses DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY*0.2 = 0.04 instead of 0.2. Only estimates change; no headers were touched.

STEP 1 (EXPLAIN ANALYZE on q09.m0): the part estimate drops from 400k to about 80k, and the join order changes completely. part⋈partsupp (436k actual) is now the build side for the lineitem probe. The orderkey join now builds on the 3.27M lineitem stream with the 15M-row orders as the probe. Total time went from about 1.2s to 0.95s in the profile.

STEP 2 (full bench): q09 went from 1211 to 709 ms (-41.4%), and a re-run gave 1096 to 702 ms (-36%). Geomean -6.5%. The other templates were within noise. q04 was +5.6% in the first run, but re-running it gave -16.1%; it has no contains filter, so its plan can't be affected.
notes: At SF10 this flips the q09 plan as the hypothesis predicted, unlike E0002 at SF1. The selectivity constant (0.04) is a heuristic. The 3-byte minimum on the literal is a guard against short, common needles flipping joins the wrong way. A possible follow-up is to scale selectivity with literal length, or to apply a similar reduction to multi-wildcard LIKE patterns (e.g. '%a%b%'), which DuckDB does not rewrite to contains(). In the new q09 plan, lineitem still gets only min/max dynamic filters, with no bloom filter on l_partkey, which may be worth looking into.

title: Per-key bloom filter for multi-key joins, revived for the post-E0008 q09 plan
summary:
Multi-key hash joins can now push a bloom filter into the probe scan for each key. Before, only single-key equality joins got one.

What changed:
- **`JoinHashTable`**: the single bloom filter is replaced by one optional filter per condition (`vector<unique_ptr<BloomFilter>>`, with `SetBuildBloomFilter`, `HasBloomFilter`, `BloomFilterCount` and `GetBloomFilter`, each taking a condition index). `AllocatePointerTable` initialises each requested filter. For single-key joins, `InsertHashes` still fills the filter from the stored row hash, so that path behaves as before. For multi-key joins, `Finalize` gathers layout column `cond_idx` (layout column i is condition i) for each chunk, hashes it with `VectorOperations::Hash` and inserts the hashes.
- **`CanUseBloomFilter`**: it now takes the condition index and accepts multi-key joins when that condition is `COMPARE_EQUAL` and its type is not nested, with at most 2 per-key filters per join. The existing `build_side_has_filter`, `probe_larger_then_build` and no-perfect-hash-table checks still apply.
- **Deferred pushes**: they are now a struct (`DeferredBloomFilter`) holding the probe info, the probe column and the condition index. `PushBloomFilter` uses that condition's filter, NULL semantics (`NullValuesAreEqual(cond_idx)`), key name and type. It is still wrapped in `SelectivityOptionalFilter`.
- **Files**: `join_hashtable.hpp/.cpp`, `join_filter_pushdown.hpp`, `physical_hash_join.cpp`.

Step 1 (profile of q09.m0): the lineitem scan now shows `l_partkey IN BF(p_partkey)` and `l_suppkey IN BF(ps_suppkey)`. It emits 3,275,523 rows instead of 60M. The 2-key join dropped from 2.44s to 0.68s CPU.

Step 2 (bench):
- **q09**: -18.9%, -15.5%, -18.4% and -13.5% across four runs (725→588, 668→564, 721→589, 711→615 ms).
- **Full bench geomean**: +0.5% on the first run, -2.0% on the second.
- **Other templates**: they swung by ±10–34% from run to run in both directions, and every one returned to the noise band on re-run (q16 went +11%, then +34%, then +1%; q05 went +11.5%, then -13.6%). q18, q19 and q22 were neutral or faster on re-check. I checked the plans for q05 and q16: q05's only multi-key join builds on an unfiltered table, so no filter is built there, and q16 has only single-key joins. Neither plan can be affected by this change.

Correctness: I compared a two-key join on an integer and a text key against a version written so it cannot get the filter. Both returned 133118 rows.
notes:
- **Header changes**: they were unavoidable. `join_filter_pushdown.hpp` now has a `DeferredBloomFilter` struct, and the `CanUseBloomFilter`/`PushBloomFilter` signatures changed. The full rebuild finished within one build call.
- **Bench noise**: this round, any single template could swing ±10–35% between runs. Any +X% result should be re-run before it is treated as a regression.
- **q09 follow-up**: the o_orderkey join (1.73s CPU, 15M-row build on orders, 3.27M probe rows) is now the biggest cost in q09. Flipping its build side or pushing a filter into orders could be the next step.
- **Second key filter**: in q09 both keys get a filter. The l_suppkey one is unselective and should switch itself off at runtime, but whether it does was not measured separately.

title: Derive per-table OR filters when the OR sits under a root AND (JoinDependentFilterRule after distributivity)
summary:
I changed only src/optimizer/rule/join_dependent_filter.cpp. The derivation logic now lives in a file-local static DeriveFilter(BoundConjunctionExpression&). It keeps the old eligibility check and returns nullptr when it can't derive anything. Apply still requires a filter or any-join operator and a root expression. A root OR behaves as before, except the derived per-table ORs are now appended as separate children of the result AND instead of being nested under one AND. A root AND is new: the rule runs DeriveFilter on each direct OR child and appends a derived conjunct only if no existing child, and no conjunct already added in this pass, is Equals() to it. Then it returns a copy of the AND and sets changes_made. No matcher change was needed: the existing SOME-child conjunction matcher already matches an AND with an OR child.

Checks: EXPLAIN ANALYZE of q19.m0 now shows the p_size/p_brand/p_container OR as a filter above the part scan (part goes from 2,000,000 rows into the build to 4,862). The lineitem scan now has the l_quantity OR as a pushed-down filter, plus a join bloom filter on l_partkey. Lineitem rows out of the scan drop from 14,994,611 to 82,782, and the top FILTER time goes from 0.38s to 0.00s.

Bench (2 bindings per template, results checked by the tool): q19 347.1 -> 185.6 ms (-46.5%), geomean -6.2%. Other templates moved between -5.7% and +1.5%, which the tool rates as noise. q07 was unchanged (+0.6%).

Planning finished with correct results on q19, q07, a nested-OR query over part/partsupp with OR-of-ANDs inside ANDs alongside a second OR conjunct (count 64407), and a root-OR nation self-join (count 1, as expected).
notes:
Termination depends on the Equals dedupe. Derived ORs hold only single-table branches, so DeriveFilter rejects them as ineligible, and the original OR's children have already been through the other rules, so a re-derivation is structurally equal to what was added. I also flattened the root-OR path's output into individual conjuncts. Without that, the AND path would see that output on the next fixpoint pass as one nested AND that doesn't match the individual derived ORs, and would add them again as duplicates.

q07 did not gain. Its nation OR is probably already handled elsewhere, or doesn't reach this shape.

Follow-up idea: derive from ORs nested deeper than the direct children of the root AND.

title: Deliminator: drop the delim join for SEMI/ANTI subqueries without blocking operators even when the LHS has a selection
summary:
I changed one file, src/optimizer/deliminator.cpp. Deliminator::Optimize keeps the deepest join with the DelimGet when the left side has a selection. It now skips that when two things are true: the delim join is SEMI or ANTI, and its right subtree has no blocking or deduplicating operator. The operators checked are aggregate/group-by, window, limit, order-by, top-n, distinct, and a nested delim join. A new file-local static recursive helper, HasBlockingOperator, does that check; no header changed. In those cases the plan falls back to the existing removal path, the one already used when the left side has no selection. EXISTS and NOT EXISTS then become a single hash SEMI/ANTI join.

Bench (your build vs current best, two runs):
- q04: 325.9 → 224.1ms (-31.2%), then 292.7 → 203.7ms (-30.4%).
- q22: 172.2 → 141.6ms (-17.8%), then 169.9 → 131.9ms (-22.4%).
- Geomean: -4.6% over all visible templates.
- The first full run showed q16 at +11.6% and q19 at +9.5%. Neither has a correlated subquery, so this change can't touch their plans. On rerun they came in at -1.7% and +3.2%, so it was noise.

The q04 profile now shows a single HASH_JOIN RIGHT_SEMI between the filtered orders scan and lineitem, with no RIGHT_DELIM_JOIN, DELIM_SCAN or dedup HASH_GROUP_BY. I checked small hand-built inputs against hand-worked answers, and all were correct:
- NOT EXISTS with NULL keys on both sides
- EXISTS and NOT EXISTS with an extra correlated inequality
- NOT EXISTS with an IS NOT DISTINCT FROM correlation
notes: The q04 semi join's condition is still `o_orderkey IS NOT DISTINCT FROM o_orderkey`, inherited from the delim join. The lineitem scan shows no dynamic or bloom filter pushed down from the semi join's build side. A follow-up could turn NOT DISTINCT FROM into plain equality for SEMI joins, which is safe for SEMI because a NULL outer key never matches under EXISTS semantics. It is not safe for ANTI with no IS NOT NULL handling, so be careful there. That could let a join filter or min-max filter prune the large probe-side scan, which still costs about 1.9s of cumulative scan time in q04. I didn't try MARK joins, since the issue scoped them out.

title: Join filters (min-max + bloom) for RIGHT_SEMI/RIGHT_ANTI probes and equality for deliminated EXISTS conditions
summary:
The change is in three .cpp files (no headers) and builds. The only clear gain is q22, about 12–30% faster across runs. q04, the main target, is flat. All other visible templates are within noise on reruns.

1. join_filter_pushdown_optimizer.cpp: GenerateJoinFilters no longer returns early for RIGHT_SEMI and RIGHT_ANTI. Their output comes from the build side and depends only on which build rows found a match, so probe rows with no matching key can be dropped. MARK, SINGLE, LEFT, OUTER and ANTI still return early. compute_aggregates_anyway stays INNER-only.
2. deliminator.cpp: when a delim join is fully deliminated, its type is INNER, SEMI or ANTI, and every removed correlation condition was a plain `=` on column refs, the `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` conditions become `=`. Those removals already added IS NOT NULL filters on the subquery-side columns. A condition is converted only if two checks pass:
   - Its RHS column ref traces back to one of those filtered columns, through column-ref projections and aggregate group keys.
   - The subquery side has only operators that cannot add NULLs: projection, filter, get, cross product, order by, limit, top-n, distinct, window, aggregates with one grouping set, and inner/semi/anti/right-semi/right-anti comparison joins.
3. compress_comparison_join.cpp (not in the plan): for RIGHT_SEMI/RIGHT_ANTI joins, the join-key columns are no longer compressed. Without this, parts A and B had no effect on q04. Compressed materialization runs before join filter pushdown and wraps the probe key in `__internal_compress_integral`, which the pushdown cannot pass through. Payload columns are still compressed.

Measured on q04.m0: the join condition went from `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` to `=`. The lineitem scan now gets min/max plus a bloom filter on the key. Rows into the join fell from 37.9M to 1.7M, and join CPU from 0.83–0.90s to 0.30s. But the scan's CPU rose by about as much, since the bloom filter is checked on all 60M rows. So q04 wall time is flat: +1%, +4%, -5% across bench runs.

Last full bench: q22 -11.7% (earlier runs -18% and -30%), geomean -1.7%. q02, q03 and q07 showed +5–8% once, and reran at -3%, -3% and 0%. q16–q19 showed +16–30% once and were within noise on rerun.

Correctness: each check was compared against a run with join_filter_pushdown, deliminator and compressed_materialization all disabled, and all matched:
- EXISTS and NOT EXISTS with NULL keys on both sides, in both directions.
- IN and NOT IN.
- NOT EXISTS with `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` in the correlation.
- A ROLLUP inside a correlated subquery.
- A UNION ALL inside NOT EXISTS.
- A LATERAL join.
- On the benchmark tables: a RIGHT_ANTI case (NOT EXISTS with a selective inner filter, so the build has keys missing from the probe), an IN subquery, and an EXISTS.
notes:
- Main surprise: compressed materialization (inside STATISTICS_PROPAGATION, which runs before JOIN_FILTER_PUSHDOWN) compresses join keys of selective joins. Semi joins are selective by nature, so their keys get compressed. PushdownJoinFilterExpression cannot pass through the compress functions, so no join filter ever reaches the probe scan. The same probably silently blocks join filters for selective INNER joins, which may be worth checking. A broader fix would teach the pushdown to handle compress functions, but min/max and bloom values would then be in the compressed domain, so that is not trivial.
- q04 did not get the expected gain. The bloom filter cuts the probe rows 22x and the join CPU drops by 0.55s, but the scan CPU rises by about 1s. The remaining cost is the 60M-row scan plus the `l_commitdate < l_receiptdate` filter.
- Follow-up idea: let the bloom/min-max filter run before the residual LOGICAL_FILTER, or order the column scan so the key column is checked first and the others are fetched only for surviving rows. That would cut the date-column decoding.
- Syntax note for future tests: `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM ANY (subquery)` is not supported by this parser.

title: Perfect hash join for RIGHT joins on dense integer keys (range up to 4M)
reasons: abandoned by the implementer after investigation
summary: Implemented the perfect hash join for RIGHT joins and for dense INNER builds with ranges up to 4M. Files: perfect_hash_join_executor.cpp/.hpp, plus a hook in physical_hash_join.cpp PrepareScanHT. (1) CanDoPerfectHashJoin accepts INNER or RIGHT with one integer equality condition. Ranges over 1M (cap 4M), and every RIGHT join, need ht.Count()*2 >= range+1. (2) The build fill now skips NULL keys; before, it read garbage values for them. RIGHT joins only reach this code since this change. (3) For RIGHT joins: a uint8 matched flag per slot is set in the probe, plus a uint32 slot index per build row in scan order. (4) PropagateMatches() re-scans the data collection pinned (KEEP_EVERYTHING_PINNED) and stores found_match=true for matched rows before ScanFullOuter. I avoided keeping row pointers from finalize because I couldn't be sure the rows stay pinned until the outer scan. Measured: q13 RIGHT join CPU 2.06s -> 1.68s in EXPLAIN ANALYZE, but q13 wall time only -1.0% / -1.4% / -0.8% over three runs. The full bench was dominated by noise: run 1 showed q03 -24%, q07 -23%, q09 +11%; run 2 showed q03 +27%, q04 +33%, q22 -18%; a targeted rerun gave q03 -2.8%, q09 +0.5%. No template showed an effect I could attribute to the change. Correctness check: a RIGHT join with NULL build keys, negative keys, a 2M range at about 99.9% density, duplicate probe keys and unmatched build rows gave the hand-computed counts and sum (3,498,600 total, 501,600 unmatched).
notes: q13 is limited by the orders scan with the NOT LIKE '%..%..%' filter (3.01s CPU) and the HASH_GROUP_BY count(o_orderkey) over 15.3M join output rows (3.05s CPU), not by the join. The perfect-HT join still costs 1.68s CPU. Much of that is probably building dictionary/slice output and the decompress/compress projections, not the lookup itself. A q13 follow-up should target the LIKE-filtered scan or the group-by over join output, for example an aggregate pushed below the join or a perfect-hash aggregate on the dense key. The bench machine was very noisy this session: whole blocks of templates moved ±25% in opposite directions between back-to-back full runs. Use targeted reruns before trusting any delta. The implementation is in the saved tree and passed the one RIGHT-join test. The NULL-key validity check in TemplatedFillSelectionVectorBuild is needed for any future RIGHT, OUTER or SEMI perfect-HT work.
